content.alt: 38. The Right Voice, Getting Along - The child whose voice booms even indoors
content.text:
The child whose voice booms even indoors

At home, at restaurants, at the library—your child always talks in a big voice. You've probably felt stuck, saying "Quiet, please" over and over with the effect lasting only a moment.

A child speaks loudly because they're excited, and because they don't yet know the "right volume for here and now." Rather than simply telling them to be quieter, it's far more effective to teach them how to adjust their voice to the situation.

Curious about the plot of this loud child storybook? We take a look at the lessons of the loud child storybook through pictures. Meet the key scenes of the loud child storybook's story, too. Read the loud child storybook together with your child and talk about it. We've gathered all kinds of stories about "38. The Right Voice, Getting Along"—including voice control storybooks, public manners storybooks, and indoor manners storybooks.

content.alt: 38. The Right Voice, Getting Along - Why voice control matters
content.text:
Why voice control matters

The ability to adjust voice volume grows both a child's self-regulation and their thoughtfulness. A child who can match their voice to the time and place is welcome everywhere, and their friendships feel more at ease.

What matters isn't "always quiet" but "just right." Shout to your heart's content in the yard; whisper softly indoors. This flexibility stays with a child as confidence, not restriction.
content.caption: The key isn't always quiet, but the right voice for the time and place.

content.alt: 38. The Right Voice, Getting Along - The story of booming-voiced Toto
content.text:
The story of booming-voiced Toto

In The Right Voice, Getting Along, Toto flings the playroom door open and lets out a huge shout. His friends jump in surprise and drift away one by one, but Toto doesn't understand why.

Hori tells him, "Sounds have a right size too. Quiet-quiet inside the room, and you can be loud outside!" A whisper game for hush-hush, and "Yahoo!" out in the yard—Toto learns to adjust his voice to the situation. At nap time he shows care for his friends with a gentle "Shh, quiet-quiet." Along with Toto, a child learns the joy of voice control.
content.caption: You can be as loud as you like in the yard, and whisper softly inside.

content.alt: 38. The Right Voice, Getting Along - A sound game to play together at home
content.text:
A sound game to play together at home

Voice control is fun to learn through play. At home, try alternating a "whisper game" and a "yahoo game." Practicing very softly indoors and loudly at the playground or yard gives your child a benchmark.

When your child gets too loud, instead of "Be quiet!" try asking, "Is this a room voice or a yard voice right now?" Their ability to judge and adjust on their own grows. When they do it well, praise them: "That was a perfect room voice!"

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How do I guide a child with a very loud voice?

A. Show them, like a game, that there's a right volume for each place. Practicing both loud and soft voices together teaches them how to adjust to the situation.

Q. Will a loud child storybook help?

A. Watching the character get along nicely by using the right voice, a child learns voice control too. A loud child storybook shows how important it is to match your voice to the situation.

Q. What if my child keeps shouting indoors?

A. Rather than scolding, gently make an agreement: "In here, let's use a quiet voice." Praising them when they use the right voice grows their ability to regulate themselves.
